prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ELI LILLY & Co" (ticker LLY), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "LLY", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Eli Lilly and Company

mission.statement: Lilly unites caring with discovery to create medicines that make life better for people around the world.
mission.source: Lilly company website (About Lilly page), published as its purpose
mission.plain: Lilly invents medicines that help sick people around the world live better lives.

about.plain: Eli Lilly is a 150-year-old company from Indianapolis that invents and makes medicines. Its biggest hits today are weekly shots, Mounjaro and Zepbound, that help people with diabetes control their blood sugar and help people with obesity lose a lot of weight. It also makes medicines for breast cancer, skin diseases and Alzheimer's disease. It spends billions every year searching for new medicines.
about.customers: Patients get its medicines through doctors, pharmacies, hospitals, insurers and governments, and increasingly buy them directly through its LillyDirect service.
about.everyday: Many people know someone taking Mounjaro or Zepbound, the weight-loss and diabetes shots that are among the best-selling medicines in the world.

money.plain: weekly tirzepatide injection for type 2 diabetes
tirzepatide for obesity and sleep apnea
pill that slows a common type of breast cancer
Trulicity, Jardiance, Taltz, insulins and many others

money.part: New launches: Foundayo, Kisunla, Ebglyss, Jaypirca
money.plain: a weight-loss pill (orforglipron), an Alzheimer's drug, an eczema shot and a blood-cancer pill
a triple-acting weight-loss shot with filing planned for early 2027

result.summary: Lilly has a strong competitive advantage today: tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) is the most effective approved incretin drug, patent-protected into the 2030s, and Lilly has built the manufacturing scale and pipeline (orforglipron, retatrutide) to stay ahead. Drug moats are time-limited by patents and government price pressure, but Lilly's R&D engine and lead in the huge obesity market make its position unusually durable for a pharma company.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue rose 45% in 2025 to $65.2B and 48% in Q2 2026, but driven by volume: under its 2025 US government agreement and cash-pay programs, cash prices for obesity drugs fell from about $1,000 to the $199-$299 range per month, and Lilly expects global prices to fall by a low-to-mid-teens percentage in 2026.

moats.evidence: Patents on tirzepatide and a pipeline of approved brands (Mounjaro, Zepbound, Verzenio, Kisunla, Ebglyss) protect exclusive sales for years; Zepbound and Mounjaro are household names.
Patients doing well on a drug, and doctors familiar with dosing, tend to stay put, and payer formularies lock in coverage, but patients can switch between GLP-1 drugs fairly easily.
A medicine does not become more useful as more people take it.

Lilly has committed tens of billions of dollars to new US and European plants for incretins and spent heavily on R&D, scale that lets it supply tens of millions of patients and fund large outcome trials that smaller rivals cannot.
The US obesity and diabetes incretin market is effectively a duopoly, with Lilly at about 60.5% and Novo Nordisk about 39% at the end of 2025, though many new entrants are in late-stage trials.
LillyDirect sells Zepbound vials directly to cash-paying patients, bypassing traditional pharmacy-benefit channels that incumbents depend on.

Decades of peptide chemistry, from the first commercial insulin in 1923 to the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide and oral small-molecule orforglipron, give Lilly a hard-to-copy R&D and manufacturing capability.
Patents on tirzepatide, orforglipron and retatrutide are exclusive assets, but they expire over time and compounded or generic versions of older GLP-1s are spreading.

customers.evidence: Lilly medicines were about 60% of US incretin prescriptions in Q2 2026 (management), patients continue to choose tirzepatide for its greater weight loss than semaglutide in the head-to-head SURMOUNT-5 trial, and Zepbound demand outstripped supply in 2024.

talent.evidence: As the world's most valuable drug company Lilly can attract top scientists and has kept expanding its workforce and R&D sites; no specific employer ranking was confirmed.

product.evidence: Tirzepatide produced 20.2% average weight loss versus 13.7% for semaglutide in the SURMOUNT-5 head-to-head trial, and Lilly followed with the first oral small-molecule GLP-1 (Foundayo/orforglipron) and positive Phase 3 data for retatrutide.

competitors.name: Novo Nordisk
competitors.note: Main rival in diabetes and obesity (Ozempic, Wegovy, oral Wegovy) and insulins; figures below are from its 2025 annual report in DKK.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: Developing MariTide, a monthly obesity injection; also competes in inflammation and oncology.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Entered obesity by acquiring Metsera; competes in oncology including breast cancer (Ibrance).

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Kisqali competes directly with Verzenio in HR+/HER2- breast cancer; Cosentyx competes with Taltz.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Obesity pipeline from its Carmot and Zealand deals, plus oncology and Alzheimer's drugs.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Oncology (breast cancer), diabetes (Farxiga vs Jardiance) and an oral GLP-1 in development.

competitors.name: Merck & Co.
competitors.note: Large oncology competitor; limited overlap in cardiometabolic.

competitors.name: AbbVie
competitors.note: Skyrizi and Rinvoq compete with Taltz, Omvoh and Ebglyss in immunology; early obesity program.

competitors.name: Biogen / Eisai
competitors.note: Leqembi competes with Kisunla in early Alzheimer's disease.

competitors.name: Sanofi
competitors.note: Insulins (Lantus, Toujeo) and Dupixent versus Ebglyss in atopic dermatitis.

competitors.name: Boehringer Ingelheim
competitors.note: Private; partner on Jardiance but developing survodutide for obesity and MASH.

competitors.name: Viking Therapeutics
competitors.note: Clinical-stage developer of injectable and oral GIP/GLP-1 obesity drugs.

competitors.name: Hims & Hers Health / compounding pharmacies
competitors.note: Telehealth sellers of compounded and branded GLP-1s competing for cash-pay obesity patients.

marketShare.market: US obesity and diabetes incretin (GLP-1) medicines
marketShare.measure: prescriptions (end of Q4 2025, as reported Feb 2026)

threats: US drug-pricing pressure: the 2025 Medicare/Medicaid agreement, cash-pay price cuts and IRA negotiation could cut incretin prices faster than volumes grow.
New obesity competitors: Novo Nordisk's oral and higher-dose Wegovy and CagriSema, Amgen's MariTide, Roche, Pfizer (Metsera) and Chinese biotechs.
Compounded and, later, generic GLP-1s (semaglutide patents expire in several countries from 2026) undercutting branded prices.
High concentration: Mounjaro and Zepbound were 56% of 2025 revenue, so any safety issue or reimbursement change would hit hard.
Debt rose to $54.9B by June 2026 to fund plants and acquisitions, against $9.0B of cash.
Pipeline or launch setbacks for orforglipron (Foundayo) and retatrutide.

ceo.name: David A. Ricks
ceo.background: Lilly career executive since 1996 (ran Lilly Bio-Medicines and Lilly China); B.S. Purdue University, MBA Indiana University

c1.evidence: Lilly leads the fast-growing obesity drug market, holding about 60% of US incretin prescriptions, with tirzepatide sales of $36.5B in 2025.

c2.evidence: Patients and doctors choose tirzepatide for greater weight loss (20.2% vs 13.7% for semaglutide in SURMOUNT-5); patents, manufacturing scale and a pipeline led by orforglipron and retatrutide make this hard to copy for years.

c3.evidence: Zepbound and Mounjaro are widely known, Lilly is the world's most valuable drug company and the default leader in obesity medicine, and patients broadly recommend the drugs.

c4.evidence: Lilly's purpose to "unite caring with discovery to create medicines that make life better" runs through its reports and its push to cap insulin at $35 in 2023, but profit pressure and drug-pricing criticism remain.

c6.evidence: “Zepbound, weight-loss drugs, innovative, expensive”: the public mostly sees Lilly positively as the maker of breakthrough obesity and diabetes medicines, tempered by concerns about drug prices.

c7.evidence: Hundreds of millions of people worldwide live with obesity or diabetes; Morgan Stanley estimated incretin sales of about $79B in 2025, a market expected to keep growing for years.

c8.evidence: Incretins are being studied and approved in sleep apnea, heart failure, kidney disease, MASH and osteoarthritis pain, and Lilly is expanding into Alzheimer's (Kisunla), gene editing and new acquisitions.

m1.evidence: Ricks bet early and heavily on tirzepatide and on building manufacturing capacity before approval, and talks of treating obesity as a chronic disease for hundreds of millions of people.

m2.evidence: Ricks is a career Lilly executive, not a founder, but he has taken founder-like long-term bets such as tens of billions of dollars of new US plants and the direct-to-patient LillyDirect channel.

m4.evidence: Ricks capped out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month in 2023 and launched lower-priced Zepbound vials for cash-pay patients, but there is little public evidence on his leadership style toward employees.

m5.evidence: Under Ricks Lilly raised R&D spending and delivered tirzepatide, orforglipron, retatrutide, Kisunla and Ebglyss, building a culture of rapid drug discovery.

m6.evidence: Ricks is closely involved in R&D and manufacturing strategy, but his background is in business and marketing (Purdue B.S., Indiana MBA), not science or engineering.

m7.evidence: His insulin price caps and push to widen access to obesity drugs point to concern for patients, though Lilly still faces criticism over US drug prices.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by David Ricks at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university could be confirmed.

m8b.evidence: Ricks is known as an outspoken voice on drug pricing and policy, but he is not a widely recognised celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: Since 2017 revenue has grown from $24.5B in 2020 to $65.2B in 2025 and operating income from $6.1B to $26.3B, making Lilly the world's largest drug company by market value.

m10.evidence: Lilly spends heavily on R&D, plants and acquisitions; frugality is not part of its reputation.

c10.evidence: Its insulins, diabetes and obesity drugs treat tens of millions of people worldwide, and incretins reduce weight-related diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and sleep apnea.

p2.evidence: Discovering and proving new medicines takes a decade and billions of dollars with high failure rates, and making peptides like tirzepatide at global scale is technically demanding; obesity and Alzheimer's are among the world's biggest health problems.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 77.7% in 2020 to 83.0% in 2025 and operating margin from 24.7% to 40.4%.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive and 2025 net income was $20.6B, but at June 30, 2026 debt was $54.9B against only $9.0B of cash and short-term investments.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $6.1B in 2020 to $26.3B in 2025, with only a dip in 2023 ($6.5B vs $7.1B in 2022); operating cash flow figures were not verified here.

v1.evidence: Tirzepatide is the strongest approved weight-loss and diabetes drug, with patients losing about a fifth of their body weight on average versus about a seventh on semaglutide in a head-to-head trial.

v2.evidence: Lilly has a strong reputation as an employer in Indianapolis and the industry, but no specific top employer ranking could be confirmed.

c5.evidence: Millions of people with diabetes, obesity, breast cancer, psoriasis and Alzheimer's rely on Lilly drugs, including affordable insulin; if it vanished, patients would lose the most effective obesity drug and face shortages.
